_comment: The six book-club contenders. Numbers are from each book's Goodreads page (the edition on the Want to Read shelf). 'year' is original publication. 'kindred' lists authors on your read shelf with a real literary link, used at half weight when you haven't read the author themselves. 'discussion' is a hand-scored 0-100 for how much a group will have to argue about. 'synopsis' is a short, spoiler-free premise.

candidates.title: The Turn of the Screw
candidates.author: Henry James
candidates.synopsis: A young governess takes a position at Bly, a remote English country house, caring for two orphaned children whose uncle wants nothing to do with them. The children are charming, maybe too charming, and soon she begins seeing figures on the tower and at the windows that no one else will admit to. A short Victorian ghost story told in her own increasingly anxious words.

kindred.author: Diane Setterfield
kindred.why: Setterfield writes in James's Victorian ghost-story tradition

kindred.author: Algernon Blackwood
kindred.why: Blackwood was James's contemporary in the English ghost-story boom

candidates.discussionWhy: Are the ghosts real or is the governess unravelling? Critics have argued about this for 125 years, and your group will too.
candidates.caveat: Late-Henry-James sentences are famously dense; short, but not fast.

candidates.title: Dark Harvest
candidates.author: Norman Partridge
candidates.synopsis: Halloween, 1963, in a small Midwestern farm town. Every year the town's teenage boys are locked up for days, then turned loose on the night of the Run to hunt the October Boy, a pumpkin-headed thing that rises from the cornfields. Whoever stops it wins a way out of town. A fast, pulpy, blood-soaked Halloween fable.

kindred.author: Ray Bradbury
kindred.why: Partridge's Halloween small town is a deliberate riff on Bradbury's Something Wicked This Way Comes

candidates.discussionWhy: A town that feeds its boys to an annual Halloween ritual: conformity, violence and who benefits from tradition. Bram Stoker Award winner.
candidates.caveat: Pulpy second-person voice and a lot of gore; plays more like a movie than a novel.

candidates.title: Pet Sematary
candidates.author: Stephen King
candidates.synopsis: Doctor Louis Creed moves his young family to a quiet house in rural Maine. There's a busy road out front, and a path in the woods behind the house leads to a cemetery where local kids have buried their pets for generations. An elderly neighbor hints that there's something older beyond it. A slow-building novel about grief, and how far a parent might go.

kindred.author: Algernon Blackwood
kindred.why: King borrowed Blackwood's Wendigo as the thing behind the burial ground

candidates.discussionWhy: The best-known horror novel about grief. Would you walk up that path? What do we owe the dead, and what do we tell our kids about death?
candidates.caveat: The longest pick by far, and the death of a child is central. Check the room before proposing it.

candidates.title: The Halloween Tree
candidates.author: Ray Bradbury
candidates.synopsis: On Halloween night, eight costumed boys set out to meet their friend Pipkin, who never shows up. A mysterious figure, Mr. Moundshroud, sweeps them off on a trip through time and around the world, from ancient Egypt to Druid Britain, medieval Paris and Mexico's Day of the Dead, to learn where Halloween's costumes and customs came from. A short, lyrical fable for all ages.
candidates.discussionWhy: A whirlwind tour of how cultures (Egypt, Celtic Britain, Notre-Dame, Día de Muertos) have faced death. Good for comparing traditions.
candidates.caveat: Written for young readers, so there's less to chew on for adults than the others.

candidates.title: Harvest Home
candidates.author: Thomas Tryon
candidates.synopsis: Ned Constantine, a New York artist, moves his wife and daughter to Cornwall Coombe, a picture-perfect New England farming village that seems untouched by the modern world. The villagers welcome them warmly and live by old rhythms of planting and harvest, led by the wise Widow Fortune. As the seasons turn toward the Harvest Home festival, Ned grows curious about customs outsiders aren't meant to see.
candidates.discussionWhy: The American Wicker Man: city family, perfect New England village, corn-goddess cult. Gender power, nostalgia and 1970s back-to-the-land anxieties.
candidates.caveat: Slow-burn first half; some 1970s gender politics that will read as dated (which can itself be a discussion).

candidates.title: The Hill of Dreams
candidates.author: Arthur Machen
candidates.synopsis: Lucian Taylor, a lonely, bookish son of a poor Welsh clergyman, finds an ancient Roman hill fort outside his village and begins to have strange visions of the old Roman town. Dreaming of becoming a writer, he later moves to London to pursue it. A dreamy, hypnotic early novel about imagination and isolation from one of the founders of weird fiction.

kindred.author: Algernon Blackwood
kindred.why: Machen and Blackwood were fellow Golden Dawn members and the twin pillars of Edwardian weird fiction

kindred.author: Jorge Luis Borges
kindred.why: Borges championed Machen and picked him for his own 'Library of Babel' anthology series

candidates.discussionWhy: A lonely young writer, a Roman ruin in Wales and a mind dissolving into visions. Is it horror at all? A good debate about art and isolation.
candidates.caveat: Hardly any plot, and hard to find in stores: only about 1.5k Goodreads ratings.
